a2-mdma: Once their jaw tenses, that should be their last dose of MDMA, so get them to slow down and cool off. If they drink a lot of plain water, even a single normal MDMA dose raises the risk of their sodium dropping too low, so have them sip an electrolyte drink when they're thirsty instead. Plain water is the risk because the drug keeps them from peeing out the extra, so it thins out the salt in their blood. Women are most at risk of this, based on the results we have: at a rave in the Netherlands, sodium was mildly low in 1 in 4 of the women on ecstasy vs only 3% of the men. California's poison control found the same pattern in the MDMA cases it got, with women at four times the odds. The following indicators would justify calling medics: If their confusion or headache worsens, or vomiting won't stop (sodium might be too low by then for an electrolyte drink to fix; while you wait for medics, if they're alert and not vomiting, give them something very salty instead, like strong broth). That has to be a lot of salt, more than a snack gives: guidelines for hikers who drank too much water use three or four bouillon cubes in half a cup of water. If their muscles keep getting weaker or their heart palpitations keep getting stronger, that could be from dangerously low potassium, like my second wife had. A seizure or collapse can result from low sodium, magnesium or potassium, and can also come from overheating or MDMA toxicity.
a2-dance: That's why I'd tell everyone not to dance on MDMA at all, however good the music is, since dancing makes the heat and the sweat that drain their salt. And really, what's the point of MDMA if someone wants to dance? For that they can take some San Pedro cactus or mescaline, which is way way safer, and still very therapeutic. Real MDMA, the kind that's therapeutic and helps people access very early childhood trauma, possibly better than San Pedro can in some cases, isn't the kind people want to dance on, which is why you don't see people in the MAPS trials of MDMA therapy saying "I NEED TO DANCE!" No, they're sitting there doing the therapy, and even if the science isn't clear on this yet, I and everyone I know are totally clear about what the real thing feels like. It's not like "I don't feel like dancing", it's like "I can barely move", couch lock. So if a pill makes someone feel like dancing, I'm highly suspicious that it contains amphetamines, or that it isn't real MDMA at all, maybe 6-APB, a similar drug. That might also be why women get low sodium far more often than men outside the lab, where what people take as "MDMA" is ecstasy, while a lab study that gave people pure MDMA and water found no difference between them. The lab also dosed everyone by their weight, though, so it couldn't show how much harder the same pill hits a smaller body.
